---
title: Recommendations
description: "Score an eligible product or content candidate using customer context and earlier interactions."
engine: markdown
---

Suppose an online shop has customer interaction logs, product metadata, and
records of the products actually displayed in each recommendation request.
It wants to rank eligible products for the next display. One observation
will describe a customer, one candidate product, and the history known when
that candidate was displayed.

For this design, `clicked_in_session` is true if the customer clicked that
logged impression before the session ended. A displayed product with no click
receives `false` after the observation window closes. The task is candidate
scoring from logged feedback.

## Describe one candidate decision

At the cutoff immediately before the display, the candidate's price and
category are known. The history contains only earlier interactions; the
current impression and its later click are outside it. For example:

```yaml
candidate_item_id: item-42
candidate_category: running_shoes
candidate_price: 89.00
events:
  - at: "2026-05-28T09:00:00Z"
    age_hours: 1
    item_id: item-17
    category: running_shoes
    action: view
  - at: "2026-05-28T09:45:00Z"
    age_hours: 0.25
    item_id: item-42
    category: running_shoes
    action: cart
clicked_in_session: true
```

This historical training row has a 10:00 cutoff. Its label is attached after
the session closes. Keep a request identifier, impression identifier, customer
identifier, and cutoff alongside the model fields so candidate scores can be
grouped back into the right ranking decision.

## Build a candidate scorer

Declare the candidate's field types, the repeated interaction context, and
the click objective together. These declarations generate the neural scorer
for this observation structure:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    candidate_item_id=rf.Hash,
    candidate_category=rf.Category,
    candidate_price=rf.Number,
    events=rf.Branch(
        length=64,
        overflow="tail",
        reduction=None,
        at=rf.DateParts(dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"]),
        age_hours=rf.Number,
        item_id=rf.Hash,
        category=rf.Category,
        action=rf.Enum(values=("view", "cart", "purchase")),
    ),
    clicked_in_session=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
```

The candidate fields describe what is being ranked; the event branch supplies
the customer's earlier behavior. Order events oldest to newest so the cap
retains the latest 64. Matching Hash configurations provide an
identity-equality signal between a candidate and history items, including
IDs absent from training. Category fields provide learned categorical context;
price, actions, and elapsed time add other evidence.

`reduction=None` keeps the history's encoded tokens available at the root for
candidate comparisons. It increases the root's token count and compute cost.
A reduced history is another configuration to evaluate, but a compact summary
can lose item-level identity detail. The
[identity](../datatypes/hash.qmd) and
[retrieval capacity evidence](../evidence/relational/retrieval-capacity.html)
explain why an equality representation alone does not guarantee successful
retrieval.

Prediction requests omit `clicked_in_session`. Each row returns that
candidate's score under `predictions.clicked_in_session`. The application
scores an eligible candidate set, groups results by request, and sorts them.
Evaluate probability calibration separately if the numeric score is used as
a click-rate estimate. After training and validation, the saved scorer can
serve these predictions through the [HTTP interface](../guides/serving.qmd)
in the application's serving infrastructure.

## Keep retrieval and ranking explicit

A large catalog usually needs a candidate-generation stage before an expensive
scorer evaluates a smaller set. The separation is illustrated by
[YouTube's candidate-generation and ranking design](https://research.google/pubs/deep-neural-networks-for-youtube-recommendations/).
For this example, your application supplies that candidate set using its
catalog, availability rules, and existing retrieval method.

The model declaration constructs a scorer for the supplied rows. Candidate
retrieval, diversity rules, inventory filtering, and final list assembly
remain application decisions. Scoring many candidates also repeats customer
context across rows; measure that cost at the actual candidate count.

Exported context vectors can support experiments with separate retrieval
systems, but their similarity must be evaluated for that purpose. See
[Representation learning](representation-learning.qmd).

## Construct labels from the available feedback

An item that was never displayed has no observed click outcome for that
impression task. Define negatives from displayed, unclicked impressions, or
explicitly formulate a different sampled-candidate objective and record its
sampling policy. For rating prediction, a missing rating is not a zero rating.

Preserve which candidates were eligible, displayed, and at which positions.
Historical exposure reflects the previous system's decisions. Offline scores
therefore describe the logged feedback population, and may change when the
serving policy changes. This selection issue is discussed in
[Recommendations as Treatments](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v48/schnabel16.html).
Use a controlled online evaluation to assess changes in customer behavior.

Split by later requests and keep all candidates from a request together.
Construct every history at that request's cutoff. Report performance for
returning users, new users, familiar items, and new items when those cohorts
matter. The item metadata supplies context for unfamiliar IDs; identity alone
does not describe a new product's appeal.

## Compare complete ranked decisions

Start with popularity or recent category preference, then compare with an
existing candidate scorer using the same feedback and candidate sets.
For a next-item retrieval experiment, compare with a suitable collaborative
filtering baseline as well. Keep the objective and negative-sampling policy
consistent across the comparison.

Evaluate ranking within each request using metrics such as NDCG@K and recall@K,
with an explicit relevance definition. Impression-level AUROC or log loss
alone does not measure a complete top-K list. Observe latency and memory at
the chosen history length, candidate count, and traffic volume.

The same structure can score content, offers, or marketplace listings when
their eligibility, feedback, and exposure are defined. A purchase target
needs its own attribution window; changing the label from a click to a purchase
changes the task. Follow [Prepare observations](../learn/prepare-observations.qmd)
and [Train and save](../learn/train-and-save.qmd) with application-owned files
for that schema.
